newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Organon denies fresh pill risk allegations.
newsitem.headline: Organon denies fresh pill risk allegations.

text.p: Akzo Nobel NV's pharmaceutical unit Organon on Friday denied a fresh spate of allegations that its high-selling low-dosage contraceptive pills doubled the risk of dangerous blood-clotting.

Organon said new tests conducted by researchers at Maastricht University indicating a link between synthetic hormones in the pills and an increased risk of thrombosis were not yet accepted and based on faulty methods.
"All established laboratory tests for thrombosis fail to show any differences between those women using the pill and those who are not," Organon said in a statement.

Dutch daily De Volkskrant said the Maastricht laboratory tests confirmed earlier research indicating that the so-called third-generation oral contraceptive 'mini-pill' doubled the chances of thrombosis.

Organon, manufacturer of top-selling mini-pill brands Mercilon and Marvelon, said earlier this year that consumer worries about the pill's health risks had cost it 70 million guilders ($36.2 million) in lost operating revenues in 1996.
Prescription of the pills is subject to restrictions in the United Kingdom, Germany and Norway, but these measures have not been adopted by the European registration authority CPMP.

Referring to a 1997 study published in prestigious British medical journal The Lancet, Organon said that latest epidemiological research had shown no differences in thrombosis risk between second- and third-generation oral contraceptives.
It said that a study of the Maastricht research results led it to conclude that the test was new rather than accepted practice and could not determine the risk of thrombosis.
Moreover, the test was based on a laboratory situation and gave no indication of the significance for women in practice, Organon said.

"Past (experience) has shown that such tests are generally unable to indicate an increased risk of thrombosis," Organon said, adding "it should be noted that the risk of thrombosis through pill use has fallen rather than risen in recent decades."
On the Amsterdam Stock Exchange shares in parent Akzo had fallen 7.20 guilders to 258.00 by 0905 GMT.
Dealers said the renewed scare had hit the stock hard.
